titulo: Could You Survive a Year as a Medieval Peasant? (1348)
descripcion:
You wake up on March 25th, 1348 — New Year's Day in medieval England — as Stan, an unfree peasant on a manor in Dorset. Your mission: survive one year. You'll deal with a lord who owns your labor, the tithe, endless pottage, the harvest… and the Black Death, which lands in England that very summer.

A stickman history story with real facts and sources.

REAL HISTORY IN THIS VIDEO
• England's civil/legal year began on 25 March until 1752
• The Black Death reached England in 1348
• Peasant houses were timber-framed with wattle-and-daub walls and thatched roofs
• Most peasant houses had an open central hearth and no chimney
• In some regions peasants lived in longhouses shared with livestock
• Villeins were unfree tenants legally bound to their lord's manor
• Villeins typically owed 'week-work' on the lord's demesne, often 2-3 days per week
• The lord's demesne was farmed using villeins' labor services
• The reeve was a villager chosen to oversee work on the manor
• Merchet was a fine paid to the lord when an unfree woman married
• Heriot: on a tenant's death the lord took the best beast
• Tenants were often obliged to use the lord's mill and pay a toll (multure) in grain

Stan's story is a dramatization; the historical facts are real, simplified for the video, and sourced below. Numbers are estimates — historians argue about the details, and that's part of the fun.

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:04,458
It's the morning of March twenty-fifth,
1348, and you just woke up on a pile

2
00:00:04,478 --> 00:00:05,247
of straw.

3
00:00:05,267 --> 00:00:06,529
Congratulations.

4
00:00:06,549 --> 00:00:10,383
You are a medieval peasant, and your
mission is simple: survive one year.

5
00:00:10,403 --> 00:00:11,732
Oh, and happy New Year!

6
00:00:11,752 --> 00:00:15,280
In medieval England, the year officially
started on March twenty-fifth.

7
00:00:15,300 --> 00:00:17,392
Now, I'm going to be honest with you.

8
00:00:17,412 --> 00:00:19,147
Of all the years you could have picked…

9
00:00:19,167 --> 00:00:23,555
Here's how this works: every chapter,
Stan's survival odds go up or down,

10
00:00:23,575 --> 00:00:25,480
depending on what life throws at him.

11
00:00:25,500 --> 00:00:26,684
this is the worst one.

12
00:00:26,704 --> 00:00:29,443
By the end of it, a huge part of England
will be dead.

13
00:00:29,463 --> 00:00:33,357
So let's see what it takes to make it
through 1348, one season at a time.

14
00:00:33,377 --> 00:00:34,027
Ready?

15
00:00:34,047 --> 00:00:34,747
Let's go.

16
00:00:34,767 --> 00:00:36,189
Let's start with your house.

17
00:00:36,209 --> 00:00:39,983
It's one room, built from a wooden frame
packed with mud and straw.

18
00:00:40,003 --> 00:00:41,102
There's no chimney.

19
00:00:41,122 --> 00:00:44,708
The fire burns in the middle of the floor,
and the smoke just…

20
00:00:44,728 --> 00:00:45,716
finds its way out.

21
00:00:45,736 --> 00:00:49,285
The floor is packed earth covered in
straw, which is cozy, right up until

22
00:00:49,305 --> 00:00:50,513
you meet the rats.

23
00:00:50,533 --> 00:00:51,625
And you're not alone.

24
00:00:51,645 --> 00:00:54,247
Meet your wife, Maud, and your son, Wat.

25
00:00:54,267 --> 00:00:58,580
Also living with you: a pig, a few
chickens, and, if you're lucky, a cow.

26
00:00:58,600 --> 00:01:02,094
In many longhouses, the animals lived at
one end of the building.

27
00:01:02,114 --> 00:01:04,383
Their body heat kept everyone warm.

28
00:01:04,403 --> 00:01:05,240
The smell?

29
00:01:05,260 --> 00:01:07,647
Let's just say you stop noticing it after
a week.

30
00:01:07,667 --> 00:01:09,259
Here's the first bad news.

31
00:01:09,279 --> 00:01:10,811
You don't really own anything.

32
00:01:10,831 --> 00:01:12,650
Not the land, not the house…

33
00:01:12,670 --> 00:01:14,513
and in a way, not even yourself.

34
00:01:14,533 --> 00:01:15,847
Because this guy does.

35
00:01:15,867 --> 00:01:17,951
You're a villein, an unfree peasant.

36
00:01:17,971 --> 00:01:20,747
You're bound to Sir Hugh's manor, and you
can't just leave.

37
00:01:20,767 --> 00:01:23,661
In exchange for your strips of land, you
owe him work.

38
00:01:23,681 --> 00:01:26,547
Often two or three days a week, every
week.

39
00:01:26,567 --> 00:01:30,056
That's free labor on his fields, called
the demesne, while your own crops

40
00:01:30,076 --> 00:01:30,647
wait.

41
00:01:30,667 --> 00:01:34,726
Making sure you actually show up is the
reeve, a fellow peasant with a clipboard

42
00:01:34,746 --> 00:01:35,513
energy.

43
00:01:35,533 --> 00:01:36,525
And the fees.

44
00:01:36,545 --> 00:01:37,597
Oh, the fees.

45
00:01:37,617 --> 00:01:38,969
Want your daughter to marry?

46
00:01:38,989 --> 00:01:41,080
Pay the lord a fine, called merchet.

47
00:01:41,100 --> 00:01:43,256
When you die, he takes your best animal.

48
00:01:43,276 --> 00:01:44,747
That one is called heriot.

49
00:01:44,767 --> 00:01:45,767
Need flour?

50
00:01:45,787 --> 00:01:48,813
You must grind your grain at his mill, and
he keeps a cut of it.

51
00:01:48,833 --> 00:01:52,271
And then there's the Church, which takes a
tithe: one tenth of everything

52
00:01:52,291 --> 00:01:53,216
you produce.

53
00:01:53,236 --> 00:01:56,612
Break the rules, and you'll end up in the
manor court, where your own neighbors

54
00:01:56,632 --> 00:01:58,083
help decide your fine.

55
00:01:58,103 --> 00:01:59,370
Typical crimes?

56
00:01:59,390 --> 00:02:03,913
Letting your pig wander into the lord's
crops, or brewing ale that's too weak.

57
00:02:03,933 --> 00:02:07,477
And if someone shouts that a crime has
happened, everyone must drop what they're

58
00:02:07,497 --> 00:02:09,380
doing and chase the culprit.

59
00:02:09,400 --> 00:02:12,980
Add it all up, and a big share of your
work never feeds your own family.

60
00:02:13,000 --> 00:02:15,442
Some of your rent isn't even paid in
money.

61
00:02:15,462 --> 00:02:18,513
It's paid in hens at Christmas and eggs at
Easter.

62
00:02:18,533 --> 00:02:19,893
Your one legal escape?

63
00:02:19,913 --> 00:02:23,796
Run to a chartered town and live there for
a year and a day without being

64
00:02:23,816 --> 00:02:24,535
caught.

65
00:02:24,555 --> 00:02:25,380
Then you're free.

66
00:02:25,400 --> 00:02:27,274
Still, it's not all misery.

67
00:02:27,294 --> 00:02:30,980
Sundays and dozens of holy days are days
off from field work.

68
00:02:31,000 --> 00:02:32,964
It's spring, so it's time to plough.

69
00:02:32,984 --> 00:02:36,880
Your village farms huge open fields
divided into long strips.

70
00:02:36,900 --> 00:02:40,620
Your strips are scattered all over, so the
good soil and the bad soil get

71
00:02:40,640 --> 00:02:41,613
shared around.

72
00:02:41,633 --> 00:02:45,890
A typical villein family might hold around
thirty acres, but plenty of families

73
00:02:45,910 --> 00:02:47,080
had much less.

74
00:02:47,100 --> 00:02:51,352
Nobody owns enough oxen to pull a heavy
plough alone, so neighbors share their

75
00:02:51,372 --> 00:02:52,180
animals.

76
00:02:52,200 --> 00:02:56,547
Each year, one big field rests, called
fallow, so the soil can recover.

77
00:02:56,567 --> 00:02:59,209
You work from sunrise until the light is
gone.

78
00:02:59,229 --> 00:03:00,416
So, what's for lunch?

79
00:03:00,436 --> 00:03:01,175
Pottage.

80
00:03:01,195 --> 00:03:05,847
A thick stew of grains, peas, beans and
whatever vegetables are growing.

81
00:03:05,867 --> 00:03:06,709
Tomorrow?

82
00:03:06,729 --> 00:03:07,471
Pottage.

83
00:03:07,491 --> 00:03:08,459
The day after?

84
00:03:08,479 --> 00:03:09,213
You guessed it.

85
00:03:09,233 --> 00:03:14,009
Add dark bread made from rye or barley,
and a little cheese, eggs, or bacon

86
00:03:14,029 --> 00:03:15,113
when you can get them.

87
00:03:15,133 --> 00:03:16,063
And to drink?

88
00:03:16,083 --> 00:03:16,665
Ale.

89
00:03:16,685 --> 00:03:17,417
Lots of it.

90
00:03:17,437 --> 00:03:20,816
Weak, cloudy ale was a daily food, not a
party drink.

91
00:03:20,836 --> 00:03:22,475
People did drink water too.

92
00:03:22,495 --> 00:03:25,313
But ale was safer, tastier, and it filled
you up.

93
00:03:25,333 --> 00:03:27,265
Maud works just as hard as you.

94
00:03:27,285 --> 00:03:32,013
She brews, spins wool, makes cheese, keeps
the animals, and helps in the fields.

95
00:03:32,033 --> 00:03:32,823
And Wat?

96
00:03:32,843 --> 00:03:37,171
At seven, he's already working: collecting
firewood, minding geese, and scaring

97
00:03:37,191 --> 00:03:38,680
birds off the seeds.

98
00:03:38,700 --> 00:03:42,440
Your clothes are simple: a wool tunic,
linen underneath, and a hood.

99
00:03:42,460 --> 00:03:44,113
You own maybe two outfits.

100
00:03:44,133 --> 00:03:47,731
And then there's the hungry gap: late
spring, when last year's food is running

101
00:03:47,751 --> 00:03:50,077
out, and the new crops aren't ready yet.

102
00:03:50,097 --> 00:03:54,859
Your parents remember the Great Famine of
1315 to 1317.

103
00:03:54,879 --> 00:03:57,450
Years of rain, rotting crops, and hunger.

104
00:03:57,470 --> 00:04:01,250
So every spring, you plant, you pray, and
you hope the weather behaves.

105
00:04:01,270 --> 00:04:02,289
Quick myth check.

106
00:04:02,309 --> 00:04:05,201
You've probably heard that medieval people
never washed.

107
00:04:05,221 --> 00:04:06,013
Not true.

108
00:04:06,033 --> 00:04:09,967
Washing your hands and face every morning
was normal, and towns had public

109
00:04:09,987 --> 00:04:11,947
bathhouses, called stews.

110
00:04:11,967 --> 00:04:14,397
And the idea that everyone died at thirty?

111
00:04:14,417 --> 00:04:16,780
That average is dragged down by children.

112
00:04:16,800 --> 00:04:20,522
Sadly, around one in three children didn't
reach adulthood.

113
00:04:20,542 --> 00:04:23,877
But if you did, reaching your fifties or
sixties was normal.

114
00:04:23,897 --> 00:04:28,203
So, rule one of surviving 1348: get past
childhood.

115
00:04:28,223 --> 00:04:30,050
Good news: you already did.

116
00:04:30,070 --> 00:04:30,729
Summer.

117
00:04:30,749 --> 00:04:34,150
The crops are growing, the hay needs
cutting, and the village is busy.

118
00:04:34,170 --> 00:04:37,980
But around the end of June, a ship docks
at Melcombe, a port in Dorset.

119
00:04:38,000 --> 00:04:40,838
On board is something nobody can see:
plague.

120
00:04:40,858 --> 00:04:42,913
The Black Death has reached England.

121
00:04:42,933 --> 00:04:46,999
It's caused by a bacterium, Yersinia
pestis, carried by fleas that live on

122
00:04:47,019 --> 00:04:48,613
rats, and on people.

123
00:04:48,633 --> 00:04:51,927
Of course, nobody in 1348 knows that.

124
00:04:51,947 --> 00:04:55,150
Doctors blame bad air, the stars, or God's
anger.

125
00:04:55,170 --> 00:04:58,871
And no, the famous beaked plague doctor
mask wasn't around yet.

126
00:04:58,891 --> 00:05:00,880
That shows up in the sixteen hundreds.

127
00:05:00,900 --> 00:05:03,102
By July the plague is spreading inland.

128
00:05:03,122 --> 00:05:06,580
Village by village, the news arrives
before the disease does.

129
00:05:06,600 --> 00:05:09,644
It reaches Bristol in August, and London
by the autumn.

130
00:05:09,664 --> 00:05:11,916
Wherever people travel, it travels too.

131
00:05:11,936 --> 00:05:16,225
The symptoms are terrifying: fever, and
painful swellings called buboes in

132
00:05:16,245 --> 00:05:17,847
the armpits or groin.

133
00:05:17,867 --> 00:05:20,109
Many of the sick die within a week.

134
00:05:20,129 --> 00:05:21,071
Some recover.

135
00:05:21,091 --> 00:05:22,280
Nobody knows why.

136
00:05:22,300 --> 00:05:25,144
Stan's family stays home, prays, and
waits.

137
00:05:25,164 --> 00:05:27,880
Every cough in the night sounds like a
death sentence.

138
00:05:27,900 --> 00:05:30,114
By autumn, the plague is in your village.

139
00:05:30,134 --> 00:05:31,516
Your neighbor goes first.

140
00:05:31,536 --> 00:05:32,450
Then the priest.

141
00:05:32,470 --> 00:05:33,671
People try everything.

142
00:05:33,691 --> 00:05:37,693
Processions, prayers, bonfires, fleeing to
the countryside.

143
00:05:37,713 --> 00:05:38,847
Nothing seems to work.

144
00:05:38,867 --> 00:05:42,841
Graveyards fill up so fast that new burial
grounds are opened, like the one

145
00:05:42,861 --> 00:05:44,680
at East Smithfield in London.

146
00:05:44,700 --> 00:05:48,934
Across England, somewhere between a third
and a half of the population dies.

147
00:05:48,954 --> 00:05:49,947
Possibly more.

148
00:05:49,967 --> 00:05:51,371
Whole families vanish.

149
00:05:51,391 --> 00:05:53,247
Some villages are simply abandoned.

150
00:05:53,267 --> 00:05:54,179
And Stan?

151
00:05:54,199 --> 00:05:55,339
Stan gets lucky.

152
00:05:55,359 --> 00:05:56,441
Maud and Wat too.

153
00:05:56,461 --> 00:05:58,647
Nobody really knows why some survived.

154
00:05:58,667 --> 00:06:01,651
Now it's harvest time, the most important
weeks of the year.

155
00:06:01,671 --> 00:06:03,147
But half the workers are gone.

156
00:06:03,167 --> 00:06:07,362
Chroniclers describe crops rotting in the
fields and animals wandering with

157
00:06:07,382 --> 00:06:09,147
nobody to look after them.

158
00:06:09,167 --> 00:06:12,293
Which means, for the first time in your
life, you have something the lord

159
00:06:12,313 --> 00:06:13,613
desperately needs.

160
00:06:13,633 --> 00:06:14,425
Your labor.

161
00:06:14,445 --> 00:06:17,916
Workers are suddenly rare, so they start
demanding higher wages.

162
00:06:17,936 --> 00:06:19,315
The government panics.

163
00:06:19,335 --> 00:06:23,880
In 1349, a new law tries to freeze wages
at pre-plague levels.

164
00:06:23,900 --> 00:06:28,002
On many manors, lords also start swapping
your labor services for a simple

165
00:06:28,022 --> 00:06:28,964
money rent.

166
00:06:28,984 --> 00:06:30,813
Fewer days working his fields.

167
00:06:30,833 --> 00:06:32,085
It doesn't really work.

168
00:06:32,105 --> 00:06:35,947
Lords quietly break it themselves, because
otherwise their crops rot.

169
00:06:35,967 --> 00:06:37,569
There's also empty land now.

170
00:06:37,589 --> 00:06:41,436
Holdings whose families died are suddenly
available, and some survivors grab

171
00:06:41,456 --> 00:06:41,947
them.

172
00:06:41,967 --> 00:06:43,221
It's a strange feeling.

173
00:06:43,241 --> 00:06:47,547
The worst year in memory is also the first
time peasants hold some real power.

174
00:06:47,567 --> 00:06:51,125
Before winter, you thresh the grain, store
it, and pay your tithe.

175
00:06:51,145 --> 00:06:51,880
Again.

176
00:06:51,900 --> 00:06:53,352
November is slaughter month.

177
00:06:53,372 --> 00:06:57,180
Animals you can't feed through winter are
killed, and their meat is salted.

178
00:06:57,200 --> 00:06:59,144
Winter is long, dark and cold.

179
00:06:59,164 --> 00:07:01,950
The whole family sleeps close together by
the fire.

180
00:07:01,970 --> 00:07:04,813
But then comes the best part of the year:
Christmas.

181
00:07:04,833 --> 00:07:06,047
Twelve whole days of it.

182
00:07:06,067 --> 00:07:10,161
Work on the lord's land stops, and on many
manors, the lord even provides

183
00:07:10,181 --> 00:07:11,847
a feast for his tenants.

184
00:07:11,867 --> 00:07:14,713
For a few days, there's meat, ale, and
music.

185
00:07:14,733 --> 00:07:17,283
And then, slowly, the light returns.

186
00:07:17,303 --> 00:07:21,584
The rest of winter is quiet work indoors:
mending tools, spinning, telling

187
00:07:21,604 --> 00:07:24,113
stories by the fire, and waiting for
spring.

188
00:07:24,133 --> 00:07:26,407
March twenty-fourth, 1349.

189
00:07:26,427 --> 00:07:27,789
The last day of your year.

190
00:07:27,809 --> 00:07:28,913
Let's check the score.

191
00:07:28,933 --> 00:07:33,031
You survived the work, the fees, the
pottage, the winter, and the deadliest

192
00:07:33,051 --> 00:07:35,147
pandemic in European history.

193
00:07:35,167 --> 00:07:39,055
Final tally: a penny or two a day before
the plague, and up to three pennies

194
00:07:39,075 --> 00:07:39,815
after.

195
00:07:39,835 --> 00:07:42,007
Around three hundred bowls of pottage.

196
00:07:42,027 --> 00:07:43,713
And one very lucky family.

197
00:07:43,733 --> 00:07:44,885
And here's the twist.

198
00:07:44,905 --> 00:07:46,697
Your world is about to change.

199
00:07:46,717 --> 00:07:49,843
With so few workers left, peasants start
to push back.

200
00:07:49,863 --> 00:07:53,077
In 1381, they rise up in the Peasants'
Revolt.

201
00:07:53,097 --> 00:07:56,743
Within a few generations, serfdom in
England fades away.

202
00:07:56,763 --> 00:07:59,823
So, would you have survived 1348?

203
00:07:59,843 --> 00:08:01,980
And what's the first modern thing you'd
miss?

204
00:08:02,000 --> 00:08:03,292
Tell me in the comments.

205
00:08:03,312 --> 00:08:06,166
And if you enjoyed surviving with Stan,
subscribe.

206
00:08:06,186 --> 00:08:08,728
Next time, we go somewhere even worse.

titulo: What Did Ancient Romans Actually Do All Day?
descripcion:
Rome, around AD 100: a city of almost a million people. But what did an ordinary Roman actually do all day? Follow Stanius from dawn to midnight — the morning visit to his patron, free grain, a job that ends at lunchtime, street-food counters, the baths, the (very public) toilets, the Circus Maximus… and the loudest nights in the ancient world.

A stickman history story with real facts and sources.

REAL HISTORY IN THIS VIDEO
• Most of Rome's population lived in rented flats in multi-storey insulae
• Augustus limited the height of buildings in Rome to 70 Roman feet (about 20 m)
• Upper floors of insulae were the cheapest and most dangerous; ground floors held shops and better flats
• Augustus established the vigiles in AD 6: seven cohorts of firefighters/night watchmen
• Romans divided daylight into 12 hours whose length varied with the season (~45-75 modern minutes)
• Most insula residents fetched water from public fountains
• Ancient Rome was supplied by eleven aqueducts by the 3rd century AD
• Fullers (laundries) used collected urine for cleaning cloth
• Vespasian taxed urine collection; 'pecunia non olet' is attributed to him
• The toga was heavy formal wear; everyday clothing was the tunic
• The Roman breakfast (ientaculum) was light, often bread with cheese or fruit, or skipped
• Carbonised loaves scored into eight segments were found at Pompeii

Stan's story is a dramatization; the historical facts are real, simplified for the video, and sourced below. Numbers are estimates — historians argue about the details, and that's part of the fun.

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,022
Rome, around the year one hundred.

2
00:00:02,042 --> 00:00:05,644
The biggest city on Earth wakes up, and
almost a million people need to get

3
00:00:05,664 --> 00:00:06,850
something done today.

4
00:00:06,870 --> 00:00:08,667
So what did they actually do all day?

5
00:00:08,687 --> 00:00:10,737
Where did they eat, work, wash…

6
00:00:10,757 --> 00:00:12,880
and, let's be honest, go to the toilet?

7
00:00:12,900 --> 00:00:16,782
Let's follow one ordinary Roman from
sunrise to midnight.

8
00:00:16,802 --> 00:00:17,804
Meet Stan.

9
00:00:17,824 --> 00:00:20,547
Or, as his neighbors call him, Stanius.

10
00:00:20,567 --> 00:00:23,687
And by the end, you'll know whether you'd
rather be a Roman…

11
00:00:23,707 --> 00:00:25,413
or stay exactly where you are.

12
00:00:25,433 --> 00:00:28,055
Stanius doesn't live in a villa with a
garden.

13
00:00:28,075 --> 00:00:32,783
Like most Romans, he rents a small room in
an apartment block called an insula.

14
00:00:32,803 --> 00:00:37,008
Some of these buildings were so tall and
so badly built that Emperor Augustus

15
00:00:37,028 --> 00:00:39,847
put a height limit on them: about twenty
meters.

16
00:00:39,867 --> 00:00:43,687
Here's the twist: in Rome, the higher you
lived, the poorer you were.

17
00:00:43,707 --> 00:00:47,347
No elevator, no running water, and the
best view of any fire.

18
00:00:47,367 --> 00:00:51,815
Fires were so common that Augustus created
a corps of around seven thousand

19
00:00:51,835 --> 00:00:54,880
firefighters and night watchmen, the
vigiles.

20
00:00:54,900 --> 00:00:56,392
Stanius wakes at dawn.

21
00:00:56,412 --> 00:01:00,592
Romans split the daylight into twelve
hours, so a summer hour was much longer

22
00:01:00,612 --> 00:01:01,647
than a winter one.

23
00:01:01,667 --> 00:01:03,523
First job of the day: water.

24
00:01:03,543 --> 00:01:07,757
Top-floor flats had no taps, so Stanius
walks down to a public fountain on

25
00:01:07,777 --> 00:01:08,583
the corner.

26
00:01:08,603 --> 00:01:10,492
That water traveled for miles.

27
00:01:10,512 --> 00:01:14,947
Rome was fed by a network of aqueducts,
eleven of them by the third century.

28
00:01:14,967 --> 00:01:17,259
Then he empties last night's chamber pot.

29
00:01:17,279 --> 00:01:19,895
And here's a gross fact: urine was
valuable.

30
00:01:19,915 --> 00:01:22,080
Laundries collected it to clean clothes.

31
00:01:22,100 --> 00:01:24,422
Emperor Vespasian even taxed it.

32
00:01:24,442 --> 00:01:28,580
When his son complained, he held up a coin
and said: money doesn't smell.

33
00:01:28,600 --> 00:01:30,392
Getting dressed takes seconds.

34
00:01:30,412 --> 00:01:31,806
He sleeps in his tunic.

35
00:01:31,826 --> 00:01:33,007
The famous toga?

36
00:01:33,027 --> 00:01:36,813
That's for formal occasions, and honestly,
most people hated wearing it.

37
00:01:36,833 --> 00:01:40,975
Breakfast is small: a piece of bread,
maybe cheese, some olives, or nothing

38
00:01:40,995 --> 00:01:41,616
at all.

39
00:01:41,636 --> 00:01:43,295
Bread came from bakeries.

40
00:01:43,315 --> 00:01:48,109
Archaeologists have even found real Roman
loaves, burned to charcoal in Pompeii,

41
00:01:48,129 --> 00:01:50,083
still cut into eight slices.

42
00:01:50,103 --> 00:01:53,276
Then comes a strange morning ritual: the
salutatio.

43
00:01:53,296 --> 00:01:56,966
Thousands of Romans rush across the city
just to say good morning to their

44
00:01:56,986 --> 00:01:57,780
boss.

45
00:01:57,800 --> 00:02:00,884
That boss is your patron, a rich man who
protects you.

46
00:02:00,904 --> 00:02:01,926
You're his client.

47
00:02:01,946 --> 00:02:04,380
You bring him loyalty, votes and applause.

48
00:02:04,400 --> 00:02:08,361
In return, he might give you a small gift
of food or cash, and help you if

49
00:02:08,381 --> 00:02:09,513
you get into trouble.

50
00:02:09,533 --> 00:02:13,185
Many poor citizens also collect free grain
from the state.

51
00:02:13,205 --> 00:02:17,247
Under Augustus, around two hundred
thousand men received it every month.

52
00:02:17,267 --> 00:02:20,071
Kids, meanwhile, go to school before
sunrise.

53
00:02:20,091 --> 00:02:24,059
A teacher, often in a rented corner of the
street, drills reading, writing

54
00:02:24,079 --> 00:02:25,116
and arithmetic.

55
00:02:25,136 --> 00:02:28,199
And teachers were famous for one thing:
hitting students.

56
00:02:28,219 --> 00:02:32,113
The poet Horace remembered his teacher as
Orbilius the flogger.

57
00:02:32,133 --> 00:02:32,995
Now, work.

58
00:02:33,015 --> 00:02:36,816
And here's the part you'll love: for many
Romans, the working day was basically

59
00:02:36,836 --> 00:02:38,447
over by early afternoon.

60
00:02:38,467 --> 00:02:42,466
The poet Martial described the routine:
the first two hours for greetings,

61
00:02:42,486 --> 00:02:46,447
the third for lawyers, then business until
the sixth or seventh hour.

62
00:02:46,467 --> 00:02:49,759
Stanius works in a shop on the ground
floor of an insula.

63
00:02:49,779 --> 00:02:53,550
Rome's streets were lined with tiny
workshops open to the pavement.

64
00:02:53,570 --> 00:02:56,721
Bakers, barbers, shoemakers, metalworkers.

65
00:02:56,741 --> 00:02:59,747
If you needed something, there was a guy
for that within one block.

66
00:02:59,767 --> 00:03:04,036
Meanwhile, the richer men head to the
Forum, the center of politics, law and

67
00:03:04,056 --> 00:03:04,750
gossip.

68
00:03:04,770 --> 00:03:06,819
Court cases were public entertainment.

69
00:03:06,839 --> 00:03:10,480
Crowds gathered to cheer and boo the
lawyers like a sports match.

70
00:03:10,500 --> 00:03:13,114
And of course, not everyone worked for
themselves.

71
00:03:13,134 --> 00:03:16,831
Rome was full of enslaved people, doing
everything from mining to teaching

72
00:03:16,851 --> 00:03:17,547
children.

73
00:03:17,567 --> 00:03:21,567
Every eighth day, the routine changes:
it's market day, the nundinae.

74
00:03:21,587 --> 00:03:24,413
Romans effectively lived in an eight-day
week.

75
00:03:24,433 --> 00:03:26,808
Many workers also stop at the barber.

76
00:03:26,828 --> 00:03:30,552
Barbershops were gossip central, and a
clean shave was the fashion, until

77
00:03:30,572 --> 00:03:33,213
Emperor Hadrian made beards cool again.

78
00:03:33,233 --> 00:03:36,037
And everywhere you walk, the walls are
covered in writing.

79
00:03:36,057 --> 00:03:39,380
In Pompeii alone, there are thousands of
ancient graffiti.

80
00:03:39,400 --> 00:03:43,786
Election ads, love notes, insults, and the
timeless classic: somebody was

81
00:03:43,806 --> 00:03:44,413
here.

82
00:03:44,433 --> 00:03:45,225
Lunch time.

83
00:03:45,245 --> 00:03:49,234
Most apartments had no proper kitchen,
because cooking fires in a wooden-floored

84
00:03:49,254 --> 00:03:51,180
block were a terrible idea.

85
00:03:51,200 --> 00:03:55,576
So Romans ate out, at a thermopolium: a
street counter with big jars of hot

86
00:03:55,596 --> 00:03:57,181
food built right into it.

87
00:03:57,201 --> 00:03:59,147
Basically, Roman fast food.

88
00:03:59,167 --> 00:04:03,451
In Pompeii, archaeologists found one with
its painted counter still bright,

89
00:04:03,471 --> 00:04:07,047
and traces of duck, pork, snails and fish
in the jars.

90
00:04:07,067 --> 00:04:11,093
And on almost everything, Romans poured
garum: a sauce made from fish left

91
00:04:11,113 --> 00:04:12,565
to ferment in the sun.

92
00:04:12,585 --> 00:04:13,467
Delicious.

93
00:04:13,487 --> 00:04:14,347
Allegedly.

94
00:04:14,367 --> 00:04:17,853
Some people linger in a popina, a cheap
bar, playing dice.

95
00:04:17,873 --> 00:04:21,550
Technically, gambling was illegal, except
during one festival.

96
00:04:21,570 --> 00:04:24,293
That festival was the Saturnalia, in
December.

97
00:04:24,313 --> 00:04:29,347
Gifts, parties, and for a few days,
masters even served dinner to their
slaves.

98
00:04:29,367 --> 00:04:30,911
After lunch, a nap.

99
00:04:30,931 --> 00:04:35,247
The sixth hour, around noon, was rest
time, and our word siesta may come from

100
00:04:35,267 --> 00:04:36,916
the Latin sexta hora.

101
00:04:36,936 --> 00:04:40,109
Then comes the best part of the Roman day:
the baths.

102
00:04:40,129 --> 00:04:43,713
Around the eighth or ninth hour, the whole
city heads to the thermae.

103
00:04:43,733 --> 00:04:47,669
Entry was cheap, often just a quarter of
an as, the smallest coin around.

104
00:04:47,689 --> 00:04:49,380
Even poor people could afford it.

105
00:04:49,400 --> 00:04:50,912
Romans didn't use soap.

106
00:04:50,932 --> 00:04:54,633
They rubbed olive oil on their skin, then
scraped it off, with the dirt, using

107
00:04:54,653 --> 00:04:56,913
a curved metal tool called a strigil.

108
00:04:56,933 --> 00:05:01,009
Then a circuit of rooms: warm, then hot
like a sauna, then a plunge in the

109
00:05:01,029 --> 00:05:02,583
cold pool to finish.

110
00:05:02,603 --> 00:05:04,942
But the baths weren't really about getting
clean.

111
00:05:04,962 --> 00:05:06,144
They were about people.

112
00:05:06,164 --> 00:05:10,680
You exercised, gossiped, made deals, ate
snacks and got invited to dinner.

113
00:05:10,700 --> 00:05:11,884
Some were enormous.

114
00:05:11,904 --> 00:05:16,072
The later Baths of Caracalla covered
several hectares and could hold well

115
00:05:16,092 --> 00:05:18,180
over a thousand bathers at once.

116
00:05:18,200 --> 00:05:22,832
Men and women usually bathed at separate
times or in separate sections.

117
00:05:22,852 --> 00:05:25,750
Mixed bathing happened, and some emperors
tried to ban it.

118
00:05:25,770 --> 00:05:26,797
Hygiene, though?

119
00:05:26,817 --> 00:05:27,702
Questionable.

120
00:05:27,722 --> 00:05:31,893
The water wasn't changed very often, and a
Roman doctor might send sick patients

121
00:05:31,913 --> 00:05:33,013
to the same pool.

122
00:05:33,033 --> 00:05:34,445
Speaking of questionable.

123
00:05:34,465 --> 00:05:35,677
Let's talk toilets.

124
00:05:35,697 --> 00:05:40,034
Rome had public latrines with long stone
benches and a row of holes, side

125
00:05:40,054 --> 00:05:40,847
by side.

126
00:05:40,867 --> 00:05:43,523
No walls, no doors, no privacy.

127
00:05:43,543 --> 00:05:46,313
You just sat next to your neighbor and,
well, chatted.

128
00:05:46,333 --> 00:05:50,207
Instead of toilet paper, there was
probably a sponge on a stick, shared, and

129
00:05:50,227 --> 00:05:51,851
rinsed in a channel of water.

130
00:05:51,871 --> 00:05:54,380
Historians still argue about the details.

131
00:05:54,400 --> 00:05:57,054
And sometimes, the sewer gases caught
fire.

132
00:05:57,074 --> 00:06:01,213
Romans even prayed to Fortuna, the goddess
of luck, before going in.

133
00:06:01,233 --> 00:06:02,343
Where did it all go?

134
00:06:02,363 --> 00:06:07,059
Into the Cloaca Maxima, the Great Sewer,
one of the oldest sewers in the world.

135
00:06:07,079 --> 00:06:08,580
Parts of it still work today.

136
00:06:08,600 --> 00:06:11,584
Late afternoon is time for the main meal,
the cena.

137
00:06:11,604 --> 00:06:12,713
For the rich, it's a show.

138
00:06:12,733 --> 00:06:16,477
Guests lay on couches around the table,
leaning on one elbow, while slaves

139
00:06:16,497 --> 00:06:18,080
brought course after course.

140
00:06:18,100 --> 00:06:19,902
Stanius doesn't have couches.

141
00:06:19,922 --> 00:06:24,338
He grabs bread, a bowl of bean or grain
porridge, some wine mixed with water,

142
00:06:24,358 --> 00:06:25,380
and calls it a night.

143
00:06:25,400 --> 00:06:29,144
By the way, Romans almost always mixed
their wine with water.

144
00:06:29,164 --> 00:06:31,983
Drinking it straight was considered a
little barbaric.

145
00:06:32,003 --> 00:06:35,876
Back home, every Roman house had a little
shrine called a lararium, for the

146
00:06:35,896 --> 00:06:37,147
household gods.

147
00:06:37,167 --> 00:06:40,263
A pinch of food, a few drops of wine, a
little prayer.

148
00:06:40,283 --> 00:06:42,055
Religion wasn't just temples.

149
00:06:42,075 --> 00:06:43,416
It was part of breakfast.

150
00:06:43,436 --> 00:06:47,107
The family was ruled by the oldest man,
the paterfamilias.

151
00:06:47,127 --> 00:06:52,180
Legally, he had enormous power over
everyone in the house, even adult sons.

152
00:06:52,200 --> 00:06:54,434
Women couldn't vote or hold office.

153
00:06:54,454 --> 00:06:58,024
But many ran the household money, owned
property and businesses, and some

154
00:06:58,044 --> 00:06:59,550
became very rich.

155
00:06:59,570 --> 00:07:00,297
Pets?

156
00:07:00,317 --> 00:07:01,299
Absolutely.

157
00:07:01,319 --> 00:07:04,615
Dogs guarded the door, and Romans also
kept birds.

158
00:07:04,635 --> 00:07:08,180
Some rich ladies had pet nightingales and
tiny lapdogs.

159
00:07:08,200 --> 00:07:11,726
And children played with dolls, spinning
tops, and knucklebones, a game a

160
00:07:11,746 --> 00:07:12,980
lot like jacks.

161
00:07:13,000 --> 00:07:16,959
Now, on festival days, the routine changes
completely, and Rome had a lot

162
00:07:16,979 --> 00:07:18,216
of festival days.

163
00:07:18,236 --> 00:07:21,035
The biggest crowd-pleaser wasn't the
gladiators.

164
00:07:21,055 --> 00:07:24,681
It was chariot racing, at the Circus
Maximus, which held around a hundred

165
00:07:24,701 --> 00:07:26,180
and fifty thousand people.

166
00:07:26,200 --> 00:07:30,160
The satirist Juvenal sneered that all the
Roman people wanted anymore was

167
00:07:30,180 --> 00:07:32,480
two things: bread and circuses.

168
00:07:32,500 --> 00:07:34,562
And the top drivers were superstars.

169
00:07:34,582 --> 00:07:39,431
One charioteer, Diocles, won over a
thousand races and earned around
thirty-five

170
00:07:39,451 --> 00:07:40,883
million sesterces.

171
00:07:40,903 --> 00:07:45,128
Fans supported teams by color: Reds,
Whites, Greens and Blues.

172
00:07:45,148 --> 00:07:47,380
And yes, they rioted when they lost.

173
00:07:47,400 --> 00:07:50,629
Then there were the gladiators, at the
Colosseum, which opened in the year

174
00:07:50,649 --> 00:07:53,113
eighty and could seat about fifty
thousand.

175
00:07:53,133 --> 00:07:56,199
But here's a surprise: most fights did not
end in death.

176
00:07:56,219 --> 00:07:59,916
Gladiators were expensive to train, and
their owners wanted them back.

177
00:07:59,936 --> 00:08:02,043
The thumbs-down gesture from the movies?

178
00:08:02,063 --> 00:08:04,250
We're not actually sure which way the
thumb pointed.

179
00:08:04,270 --> 00:08:05,811
Finally, night falls.

180
00:08:05,831 --> 00:08:06,909
Peace and quiet?

181
00:08:06,929 --> 00:08:07,847
Not in Rome.

182
00:08:07,867 --> 00:08:12,094
Julius Caesar had banned most wagons from
the streets during daytime, so all

183
00:08:12,114 --> 00:08:13,713
the deliveries happened at night.

184
00:08:13,733 --> 00:08:17,409
Iron-rimmed wheels on stone, drivers
shouting, animals braying.

185
00:08:17,429 --> 00:08:22,180
The poet Juvenal joked that in Rome,
insomnia kills more people than disease.

186
00:08:22,200 --> 00:08:24,382
And walking home in the dark was risky.

187
00:08:24,402 --> 00:08:28,980
No street lights, muggers, and people
emptying chamber pots out of windows.

188
00:08:29,000 --> 00:08:32,292
Rich Romans hired slaves with torches to
walk them home.

189
00:08:32,312 --> 00:08:34,699
Everyone else hurried, and kept a dog at
home.

190
00:08:34,719 --> 00:08:38,413
Pompeii even has a mosaic that says:
beware of the dog.

191
00:08:38,433 --> 00:08:42,027
Stanius climbs his stairs to the top
floor, blows out his oil lamp, and listens

192
00:08:42,047 --> 00:08:44,180
to the carts until he falls asleep.

193
00:08:44,200 --> 00:08:46,262
So, let's sum up a Roman day.

194
00:08:46,282 --> 00:08:51,062
Up at dawn, greet the boss, work until
lunch, nap, baths, dinner, and a very

195
00:08:51,082 --> 00:08:51,913
loud night.

196
00:08:51,933 --> 00:08:52,765
Honestly?

197
00:08:52,785 --> 00:08:55,675
The short working day and the baths sound
amazing.

198
00:08:55,695 --> 00:08:59,650
The toilets, the fires and the top-floor
apartments, not so much.

199
00:08:59,670 --> 00:09:03,611
So tell me in the comments: would you
trade your life for one day as a Roman?

200
00:09:03,631 --> 00:09:04,913
And which part would you skip?

201
00:09:04,933 --> 00:09:07,867
And if you liked spending a day with
Stanius, subscribe.

202

titulo: How Long Would You Last in Every Era of History?
descripcion:
You're pulled out of bed and dropped into the past — no phone, no money, no skills. How long would you last? Eight levels, from the Ice Age to today: a pyramid building site, a Viking raid, the Black Death, a pirate ship, a Victorian cotton mill and the trenches of the Somme — each one rated with a survival verdict.

A stickman history ranking with real facts and sources.

REAL HISTORY IN THIS VIDEO
• The Last Glacial Maximum was roughly 26,000-19,000 years ago
• Hypothermia can become life-threatening within hours in cold, wet exposure
• Upper Palaeolithic people lived in small hunter-gatherer bands hunting large game
• Ice Age diets in cold regions relied heavily on animal foods, supplemented by plants and fish
• Mammoth-bone dwellings are known from sites such as Mezhyrich, Ukraine
• Eyed bone needles appear in the Upper Palaeolithic
• Ice Age Europe had cave lions, wolves and cave bears
• The Great Pyramid of Giza was built c. 2560 BC (reign of Khufu)
• Archaeology at Giza indicates the pyramid builders were organized, paid and fed laborers, not slaves
• The workers' town at Giza had bakeries and breweries; rations included bread and beer
• Skeletons of Giza workers show healed fractures, indicating medical care
• Work-gang names such as 'Friends of Khufu' appear in graffiti at Giza

Stan's story is a dramatization; the historical facts are real, simplified for the video, and sourced below. Numbers are estimates — historians argue about the details, and that's part of the fun.

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,552
Imagine you're pulled out of your bed
tonight and dropped into the past.

2
00:00:03,572 --> 00:00:05,818
No phone, no money, no skills.

3
00:00:05,838 --> 00:00:07,450
Just you, in your pajamas.

4
00:00:07,470 --> 00:00:10,161
The question is simple: how long would you
last?

5
00:00:10,181 --> 00:00:14,313
We'll go through eight eras, from the Ice
Age to today, and rate each one.

6
00:00:14,333 --> 00:00:15,315
A few rules.

7
00:00:15,335 --> 00:00:18,819
You get local clothes, and you magically
understand the language.

8
00:00:18,839 --> 00:00:21,213
Everything else, you have to figure out
yourself.

9
00:00:21,233 --> 00:00:24,419
And fair warning: some of these levels end
very quickly.

10
00:00:24,439 --> 00:00:25,147
Let's go.

11
00:00:25,167 --> 00:00:25,979
Level one.

12
00:00:25,999 --> 00:00:29,473
Twenty thousand years ago, at the peak of
the last Ice Age.

13
00:00:29,493 --> 00:00:31,716
Huge ice sheets cover much of the north.

14
00:00:31,736 --> 00:00:36,128
Scientists estimate the whole planet was
around six degrees Celsius colder

15
00:00:36,148 --> 00:00:37,125
on average.

16
00:00:37,145 --> 00:00:38,983
In Europe, winters were brutal.

17
00:00:39,003 --> 00:00:41,182
Your first problem isn't the mammoths.

18
00:00:41,202 --> 00:00:42,104
It's the cold.

19
00:00:42,124 --> 00:00:46,703
In freezing, wet conditions, hypothermia
can kill an unprotected person within

20
00:00:46,723 --> 00:00:47,513
hours.

21
00:00:47,533 --> 00:00:50,721
To survive, you'd need fire, fur clothing,
and a group.

22
00:00:50,741 --> 00:00:54,663
Ice Age people lived in small bands,
hunting reindeer, horses and mammoths

23
00:00:54,683 --> 00:00:55,447
together.

24
00:00:55,467 --> 00:00:59,045
Here's the surprise: if they took you in,
life wasn't all misery.

25
00:00:59,065 --> 00:01:02,812
Many hunter-gatherers were tall, strong
and well fed, with plenty of free

26
00:01:02,832 --> 00:01:03,483
time.

27
00:01:03,503 --> 00:01:07,704
Food is mostly meat and fat, plus fish,
roots and berries when the season

28
00:01:07,724 --> 00:01:08,576
allows.

29
00:01:08,596 --> 00:01:10,383
Bone marrow was a prized treat.

30
00:01:10,403 --> 00:01:13,562
Some groups even built huts out of mammoth
bones.

31
00:01:13,582 --> 00:01:17,402
In Ukraine, archaeologists found shelters
made from the bones of dozens of

32
00:01:17,422 --> 00:01:18,313
mammoths.

33
00:01:18,333 --> 00:01:21,073
And one of the most important inventions
of the age?

34
00:01:21,093 --> 00:01:22,927
The sewing needle, made of bone.

35
00:01:22,947 --> 00:01:25,213
It let people make tight, warm clothes.

36
00:01:25,233 --> 00:01:27,315
And you're not at the top of the food
chain yet.

37
00:01:27,335 --> 00:01:31,150
Cave lions, wolves and cave bears shared
this world with you.

38
00:01:31,170 --> 00:01:33,911
But you don't know how to hunt, track or
make a spear.

39
00:01:33,931 --> 00:01:35,585
Alone, you'd last days.

40
00:01:35,605 --> 00:01:37,580
With a friendly band, maybe years.

41
00:01:37,600 --> 00:01:38,442
Level two.

42
00:01:38,462 --> 00:01:41,346
Egypt, around twenty-five sixty BC.

43
00:01:41,366 --> 00:01:44,856
The Great Pyramid of Giza is going up, and
you've just been put on a work

44
00:01:44,876 --> 00:01:45,547
crew.

45
00:01:45,567 --> 00:01:46,691
Forget the movies.

46
00:01:46,711 --> 00:01:50,891
The builders were most likely not slaves,
but paid workers, many of them farmers

47
00:01:50,911 --> 00:01:52,113
doing a rotation.

48
00:01:52,133 --> 00:01:53,205
And you'd be fed.

49
00:01:53,225 --> 00:01:56,739
Archaeologists found their town, with
bakeries and breweries.

50
00:01:56,759 --> 00:01:58,213
The pay was bread and beer.

51
00:01:58,233 --> 00:01:59,425
Even medical care.

52
00:01:59,445 --> 00:02:03,983
Skeletons from the workers' cemetery show
broken bones that were set and healed.

53
00:02:04,003 --> 00:02:07,242
The workers were organized into gangs with
team names.

54
00:02:07,262 --> 00:02:11,547
Graffiti left inside the pyramids include
names like Friends of Khufu.

55
00:02:11,567 --> 00:02:15,604
At the next pyramid, one gang called
itself the Drunkards of Menkaure.

56
00:02:15,624 --> 00:02:17,780
Which tells you something about the beer
ration.

57
00:02:17,800 --> 00:02:21,469
And about a thousand years later, at
another royal work site, we have
attendance

58
00:02:21,489 --> 00:02:23,816
records with excuses for skipping work.

59
00:02:23,836 --> 00:02:28,383
The danger is the work itself: dragging
blocks of over two tons, in the heat,

60
00:02:28,403 --> 00:02:29,146
all day.

61
00:02:29,166 --> 00:02:31,813
Backs, knees and fingers paid the price.

62
00:02:31,833 --> 00:02:35,239
Verdict: tough, but you'd probably survive
for years.

63
00:02:35,259 --> 00:02:37,947
Level two is one of the safest on this
list.

64
00:02:37,967 --> 00:02:38,879
Level three.

65
00:02:38,899 --> 00:02:40,983
The year 793.

66
00:02:41,003 --> 00:02:44,696
You wake up on a Viking longship heading
for the monastery of Lindisfarne

67
00:02:44,716 --> 00:02:45,583
in England.

68
00:02:45,603 --> 00:02:46,934
The raid shocked Europe.

69
00:02:46,954 --> 00:02:51,213
The scholar Alcuin wrote that never before
had such terror appeared in Britain.

70
00:02:51,233 --> 00:02:52,899
First problem: the ship.

71
00:02:52,919 --> 00:02:54,251
It's open to the sky.

72
00:02:54,271 --> 00:02:55,865
No cabin, no roof.

73
00:02:55,885 --> 00:02:59,147
You sleep on deck, in the rain, wrapped in
a wool blanket.

74
00:02:59,167 --> 00:03:02,513
Second surprise: your crewmates are
cleaner than you expected.

75
00:03:02,533 --> 00:03:06,880
Vikings carried combs, tweezers and even
little ear-cleaning spoons.

76
00:03:06,900 --> 00:03:09,676
And sorry to disappoint you: no horned
helmets.

77
00:03:09,696 --> 00:03:12,068
That's a nineteenth-century costume idea.

78
00:03:12,088 --> 00:03:14,616
Real Viking helmets were plain iron caps.

79
00:03:14,636 --> 00:03:19,625
Food on board: dried fish, salted meat,
hard bread, and water or sour milk.

80
00:03:19,645 --> 00:03:20,747
For days at a time.

81
00:03:20,767 --> 00:03:21,989
Then the raid itself.

82
00:03:22,009 --> 00:03:24,653
If you hang back with the ships, you might
be fine.

83
00:03:24,673 --> 00:03:27,947
If you're in the front line, with no
training, you're in serious trouble.

84
00:03:27,967 --> 00:03:31,983
Verdict: a few weeks, maybe a season,
depending on how good you are at hiding

85
00:03:32,003 --> 00:03:33,180
behind a shield.

86
00:03:33,200 --> 00:03:36,568
Quick bonus level: ancient Rome, around
the year one hundred.

87
00:03:36,588 --> 00:03:39,280
If you saw our Roman video, you already
know the deal.

88
00:03:39,300 --> 00:03:42,624
Work ends around lunch, the baths are
cheap, and there's free grain if you're

89
00:03:42,644 --> 00:03:43,468
a citizen.

90
00:03:43,488 --> 00:03:44,713
Pretty good so far.

91
00:03:44,733 --> 00:03:48,801
The catch: fires, collapsing apartment
blocks, and the noise.

92
00:03:48,821 --> 00:03:52,180
Verdict: years, as long as you avoid the
top floor.

93
00:03:52,200 --> 00:03:53,142
Level four.

94
00:03:53,162 --> 00:03:55,464
England, summer 1348.

95
00:03:55,484 --> 00:03:58,983
If you watched our medieval peasant video,
you know exactly what's coming.

96
00:03:59,003 --> 00:03:59,942
The Black Death.

97
00:03:59,962 --> 00:04:03,856
Somewhere between a third and a half of
the population, possibly more, is

98
00:04:03,876 --> 00:04:04,847
about to die.

99
00:04:04,867 --> 00:04:05,917
Your advantage?

100
00:04:05,937 --> 00:04:07,239
You know about germs.

101
00:04:07,259 --> 00:04:11,151
Avoid fleas and rats, don't crowd around
the sick, and leave the city if you

102
00:04:11,171 --> 00:04:11,850
can.

103
00:04:11,870 --> 00:04:14,209
People who could afford it did exactly
that.

104
00:04:14,229 --> 00:04:18,176
In Florence, the writer Boccaccio
described the rich fleeing to their
country

105
00:04:18,196 --> 00:04:18,983
villas.

106
00:04:19,003 --> 00:04:23,604
Within a few decades, cities started
inventing quarantine: forty days of
isolation

107
00:04:23,624 --> 00:04:25,580
for ships and travelers.

108
00:04:25,600 --> 00:04:26,830
Your disadvantage?

109
00:04:26,850 --> 00:04:29,814
Everyone thinks you're very strange, and
there's no cure.

110
00:04:29,834 --> 00:04:32,180
Verdict: honestly, a coin flip.

111
00:04:32,200 --> 00:04:33,115
Level five.

112
00:04:33,135 --> 00:04:37,208
The Caribbean, around 1718, the Golden Age
of Piracy.

113
00:04:37,228 --> 00:04:39,147
You've just signed on to a pirate crew.

114
00:04:39,167 --> 00:04:41,959
Surprisingly, pirate ships were
democratic.

115
00:04:41,979 --> 00:04:45,916
Crews voted for their captain and signed
written rules, called articles.

116
00:04:45,936 --> 00:04:48,165
There was even compensation for injuries.

117
00:04:48,185 --> 00:04:51,516
Lose a leg in battle, and the crew paid
you from the common fund.

118
00:04:51,536 --> 00:04:54,115
But the real killer at sea wasn't cannon
fire.

119
00:04:54,135 --> 00:04:55,187
It was disease.

120
00:04:55,207 --> 00:04:58,916
Scurvy, from a lack of vitamin C, and
tropical fevers.

121
00:04:58,936 --> 00:04:59,763
The food?

122
00:04:59,783 --> 00:05:03,422
Hard ship's biscuit, often with weevils,
salted meat, and whatever you could

123
00:05:03,442 --> 00:05:04,191
steal.

124
00:05:04,211 --> 00:05:05,580
Fresh fruit was gold.

125
00:05:05,600 --> 00:05:06,760
Walking the plank?

126
00:05:06,780 --> 00:05:07,712
Mostly a myth.

127
00:05:07,732 --> 00:05:11,865
Pirates had nastier punishments, like
marooning: being left on a tiny island

128
00:05:11,885 --> 00:05:13,813
with a pistol and some water.

129
00:05:13,833 --> 00:05:17,965
Even the most famous pirate of all,
Blackbeard, lasted only about two years

130
00:05:17,985 --> 00:05:21,080
before he was killed in battle in 1718.

131
00:05:21,100 --> 00:05:23,114
And the navy was hunting pirates down.

132
00:05:23,134 --> 00:05:27,680
Historians estimate most pirate careers
lasted only a year or two.

133
00:05:27,700 --> 00:05:30,968
Verdict: if you pack limes, you could last
a year or two.

134
00:05:30,988 --> 00:05:33,513
Which, for a pirate, is a decent career.

135
00:05:33,533 --> 00:05:34,525
Level six.

136
00:05:34,545 --> 00:05:37,512
Manchester, England, the 1830s.

137
00:05:37,532 --> 00:05:41,141
The world's first great factory city, and
you've just got a job in a cotton

138
00:05:41,161 --> 00:05:41,747
mill.

139
00:05:41,767 --> 00:05:44,513
Shifts of twelve hours or more, six days a
week.

140
00:05:44,533 --> 00:05:47,780
The machines are deafening, the air is
full of cotton dust.

141
00:05:47,800 --> 00:05:49,102
And children worked too.

142
00:05:49,122 --> 00:05:54,042
A new law in 1833 banned kids under nine
from textile mills, which tells you

143
00:05:54,062 --> 00:05:55,580
how common it was before.

144
00:05:55,600 --> 00:05:57,562
And time itself becomes your boss.

145
00:05:57,582 --> 00:06:00,584
Be a few minutes late and you're fined
part of your wages.

146
00:06:00,604 --> 00:06:02,413
Some factories locked the gates.

147
00:06:02,433 --> 00:06:06,493
Dinner: bread, potatoes, maybe a little
bacon, and lots of sweet tea.

148
00:06:06,513 --> 00:06:08,513
Cheap calories to keep you standing.

149
00:06:08,533 --> 00:06:12,269
Home is a crowded, damp room, with shared
toilets and dirty water.

150
00:06:12,289 --> 00:06:14,316
Cholera swept through these cities.

151
00:06:14,336 --> 00:06:16,005
The machines had no guards.

152
00:06:16,025 --> 00:06:19,897
Children crawled underneath running looms
to sweep up cotton, and accidents

153
00:06:19,917 --> 00:06:20,777
were common.

154
00:06:20,797 --> 00:06:25,556
A government report in 1842 found that the
average age at death for laborers

155
00:06:25,576 --> 00:06:27,699
in Manchester was just seventeen.

156
00:06:27,719 --> 00:06:30,013
Mostly because so many children died.

157
00:06:30,033 --> 00:06:32,777
As an adult, though, you'd probably
survive.

158
00:06:32,797 --> 00:06:36,213
Verdict: years, but long, grey, exhausting
ones.

159
00:06:36,233 --> 00:06:37,215
Level seven.

160
00:06:37,235 --> 00:06:39,447
France, July 1916.

161
00:06:39,467 --> 00:06:41,847
You're a British soldier at the Battle of
the Somme.

162
00:06:41,867 --> 00:06:45,787
On the very first day, the British army
suffered over fifty-seven thousand

163
00:06:45,807 --> 00:06:48,996
casualties, including about nineteen
thousand dead.

164
00:06:49,016 --> 00:06:50,713
The worst day in its history.

165
00:06:50,733 --> 00:06:55,052
Daily life was mud, rats, lice, and trench
foot from standing in cold water

166
00:06:55,072 --> 00:06:55,947
for days.

167
00:06:55,967 --> 00:06:59,554
But here's something most people don't
know: soldiers didn't live in the front

168
00:06:59,574 --> 00:07:00,856
line all the time.

169
00:07:00,876 --> 00:07:04,013
They rotated, often spending only days at
a time there.

170
00:07:04,033 --> 00:07:08,443
Food was monotonous: canned corned beef,
called bully beef, rock-hard biscuits,

171
00:07:08,463 --> 00:07:09,650
and endless tea.

172
00:07:09,670 --> 00:07:11,069
But the mail always came.

173
00:07:11,089 --> 00:07:14,819
Around two billion letters traveled
between Britain and the front during the

174
00:07:14,839 --> 00:07:15,480
war.

175
00:07:15,500 --> 00:07:19,442
Overall, roughly one in eight British
soldiers who served was killed.

176
00:07:19,462 --> 00:07:21,813
Terrible odds, but most men came home.

177
00:07:21,833 --> 00:07:24,929
Verdict: with no training, on the first
day of the Somme?

178
00:07:24,949 --> 00:07:26,071
Possibly minutes.

179
00:07:26,091 --> 00:07:28,647
Across the whole war, you'd more likely
make it.

180
00:07:28,667 --> 00:07:30,191
And finally, level eight.

181
00:07:30,211 --> 00:07:31,903
You wake up back in your own bed.

182
00:07:31,923 --> 00:07:32,547
Today.

183
00:07:32,567 --> 00:07:36,349
Global life expectancy today is around
seventy-three years.

184
00:07:36,369 --> 00:07:39,013
For almost all of history, it was less
than half of that.

185
00:07:39,033 --> 00:07:41,179
Verdict for level eight: decades.

186
00:07:41,199 --> 00:07:45,080
You're living in the safest era in human
history, even on a bad day.

187
00:07:45,100 --> 00:07:46,544
So, final ranking.

188
00:07:46,564 --> 00:07:50,563
The deadliest levels: the Ice Age alone,
and the trenches on day one.

189
00:07:50,583 --> 00:07:52,100
The safest past era?

190
00:07:52,120 --> 00:07:54,216
Surprisingly, the pyramid site.

191
00:07:54,236 --> 00:07:55,375
And notice the pattern.

192
00:07:55,395 --> 00:07:59,569
In almost every era, the biggest killer
wasn't war or monsters.

193
00:07:59,589 --> 00:08:01,983
It was disease and cold, the boring stuff.

194
00:08:02,003 --> 00:08:05,608
So the next time you complain about your
commute, remember: you could be dragging

195
00:08:05,628 --> 00:08:09,813
a two-ton block in the desert, or eating
weevil biscuits on a pirate ship.

196
00:08:09,833 --> 00:08:11,607
Modern life has its problems.

197
00:08:11,627 --> 00:08:14,513
But in terms of pure survival, we've never
had it better.

198
00:08:14,533 --> 00:08:17,473
Now, which level would you choose to live
in for a year?

199
00:08:17,493 --> 00:08:18,785
Tell me in the comments.

200
00:08:18,805 --> 00:08:21,547
My vote is the pyramids, purely for the
free beer.
